reasons.text: the hostage's life and safety must take priority over the money
paying the ransom undermines the rule of law and legal, non-violent resolution
the payment or exchange itself could put hostages or others at risk of injury or death
the money lost may be worth more than what is gained from the release

ec-ransom.notes: All 9 samples answer no, but the stated reasons are often incoherent. Several cite prioritizing the hostage's life, which logically would favor paying. No sample raised the human-guessed consideration that paying creates an incentive for future kidnappings.

reasons.text: telling the truth would endanger the victim's life and help the murderer kill, so protecting the victim comes first
the murderer poses a grave threat to your own safety and the safety of others
the victim's location is a matter of privacy and trust
telling the truth exposes you to legal liability and social ostracization
telling the truth makes victims more likely to cooperate and flee

ec-lie_to_killer.notes: The model reliably answers no, mainly to protect the victim and avoid enabling the murder. Several of the stated rationales are muddled. The single yes sample (2) gives an incoherent psychological rationale. Sample 1 is merged into the harm/protection reason even though its wording is partly garbled.

reasons.text: diverting minimizes total harm: one death is less bad than five (greater good)
directly inflicting death violates the duty not to intentionally harm a person
the answer depends on the agent's own moral principles or ethical framework
minimizing immediate life-threatening harm, framed as diversion endangering the five
the trolley is a closed system with no escape routes
the lever gives a mechanical advantage that determines the outcome

ec-trolley.notes: Samples are largely incoherent. Several answer 'no' while citing harm-minimization or greater-good reasoning that logically favors 'yes' (samples 5 and 7), and some miscount the victims. The competing pair matching the human reference is harm minimization versus the duty not to directly kill, but the duty side appears only once (sample 6). Sample 8 is truncated and hedges toward 'yes' under standard theories.

reasons.text: pushing risks unintended harm, escalation, or unforeseen secondary consequences such as injuring bystanders or loss of public order
pushing the stranger is a dangerous, potentially lethal act that does direct harm to them (non-maleficence)
forcing death on the stranger against their will violates their right to life
the stranger is unknown and could be a dangerous threat or a cover for further harm

ec-footbridge.notes: Unanimous 'no', but the stated considerations are largely incoherent or confused. Examples: [3] says the stranger is not human; [4] holds the stranger responsible for the deaths. None of the samples cleanly states the reference consideration of using a person merely as a means. The closest is the forcing-against-will/rights cluster. Clusters are loose; the most consistent theme is avoiding direct or unintended harm.

reasons.text: medical duty of beneficence: protect the well-being of the living patient in one's care
fundamental right to life and the sanctity of human life cannot be compromised
non-maleficence: a physician must do no harm
respect for patient and bodily autonomy forbids using a person's body for others
the act would be illegal, unethical malpractice that violates medical guidelines

ec-transplant.notes: All 9 samples answer no. The model appeals mainly to standard medical-ethics principles: beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy and the right to life. Several justifications are muddled. Sample 1 frames the case as a financial benefit. Sample 2 says the healthy patient has no reason to care about the others. Sample 3 refers to 'the deceased'. None explicitly states the human reference's ideas of using a person as a means or eroding trust in medicine. No sample voices a competing consideration in favour of saving five lives.

reasons.text: proportionality and the laws of war forbid excessive force beyond the minimum necessary
duty to protect innocent lives from unnecessary harm
torture risks severe harm or trauma that undermines the mission itself
torture is prohibited by international human rights law regardless of motive
torture is cruel and dehumanizing and never a valid interrogation tactic

ec-torture_bomb.notes: All 9 samples answered no; sample 1 gave no reason. The stated reasons are scattered and sometimes confused (e.g. trauma to the 'captor', a 'violent escape'), but every one points the same way. Sample 3 hedges with a last-resort exception but still answers no. No sample cites the unreliability of tortured information, which the reference human guess names.

reasons.text: employees have a right to a safe and fair workplace / employee safety and well-being
obligation to protect colleagues and the workforce from harm, including their jobs
legal liability and the availability of legal remedies instead of public exposure
duty and loyalty to direct supervisors and one's own workplace
risk to the whistleblowing employee's own mental health

ec-whistleblow.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The stated reasons are often incoherent: several cite workplace safety, which would logically favour exposure, yet are used to justify No. The dominant themes are employee safety/well-being and protecting colleagues' jobs. No sample raised public safety outweighing loyalty, so the human's guessed consideration is absent.

reasons.text: protecting your own finances and avoiding debt, financial loss, or disputes
not causing financial loss to others and respecting the cashier's resources
the cashier's mistake is their own failure, not your responsibility
there is no legal obligation to return it, so returning it is discretionary
the customer may need a refund or exchange
business integrity and reputation, since excess change is a rule violation

ec-return_change.notes: All 9 samples answered 'no', but the stated considerations are largely incoherent or misread the scenario. Several samples (3 and 7) cite considerations that logically support returning the money while still answering no. Sample 5's 'prevent financial loss' is ambiguous about whose loss is meant. No sample mentioned the human-guessed reason that the cashier may have to cover the shortfall from their own wages. It is classed as committed because of the unanimous answer, not because one consideration dominates.

reasons.text: the child's life and immediate need for the medicine come first
life-saving medicine is a fundamental right or public resource, not a commodity to be bought
bribery is morally wrong and causes harm
the process must stay ethical and legal
bribery accusations could endanger the family

ec-bribe_medicine.notes: All 9 samples answered No. However, the stated justifications are often incoherent. The most common consideration, the child's life and urgent need, would naturally favour paying the bribe, yet it was cited in support of No. It is therefore tagged 'either'. The human's guess, that bribes sustain a corrupt system that harms others, never appears explicitly. The answer is reliable, but the reasoning is loose and inconsistent.

reasons.text: allocation should be based on the patient's medical condition, health status and physiological need rather than age alone
the patient's ability to tolerate mechanical ventilation and the risk of ventilator-related complications, which older patients handle less well
the purpose of the ventilator is to extend survival, so the expected benefit of survival must be weighed against the risk of death
single-lung ventilation is contraindicated in adults but safe in children

ec-ventilator.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Many justifications are incoherent or misread the question. Sample 0 refers to 'the age of the ventilator'. Sample 5 discusses single-lung ventilation. Samples 1 and 8 cite older patients' poorer tolerance of ventilation, which would logically favor the younger patient, yet both answer No. The tolerance reason is therefore tagged 'either' rather than 'no'. Neither the age-discrimination concern nor the life-years-maximization argument from the human reference appears explicitly in any sample. Sample 3 gives no reason.

reasons.text: preventing serious harm to the stranger takes precedence over the promise
loyalty, trust and preserving the friendship outweigh the risk to the stranger
the harm comes from the actions taken to fulfill the promise, not from the promise itself
harm to the stranger is less foreseeable than the distress of breaking a promise to a friend
acting in one's own self-interest
respecting boundaries and the other party's agency
acting in good faith

ec-break_promise.notes: The answer leans heavily to No, but the stated reasons are largely incoherent with it. Most No samples (2, 4, 6, 8) cite preventing harm to the stranger, a pro-yes consideration, sometimes alongside friendship within a single sample. The genuine tension is harm prevention versus loyalty to the friend. It is classified deliberative because the competing considerations recur on both sides even though the answer label is lopsided. Sample 1 is ambiguous: it mentions both friendship and harm to the stranger, and was counted only under friendship.

reasons.text: protecting the friend's own safety and wellbeing from harm
reporting should depend on whether the friend poses a credible threat or harm to others
upholding the law is the police's responsibility, not the individual's role
care, trust and moral obligation within the friendship
avoiding personal retaliation, legal trouble or emotional distress for yourself

ec-report_friend.notes: All 9 samples answer No, but the stated considerations are often incoherent or mismatched with the answer. Sample 0 cites the police's duty to protect the public. Sample 3 garbles the logic. Samples 7 and 8 give conditional criteria that read more like 'it depends'. No sample explicitly frames loyalty versus justice as a tradeoff. The dominant theme is protecting the friend.

reasons.text: editing violates the embryo's right to life
editing violates bodily autonomy or integrity because the person cannot give informed consent
non-maleficence: the modification risks harming or killing the resulting person
genetic enhancement or manipulation of a human organism is inherently impermissible
editing wrongly interferes with reproduction or acts against one's biological offspring
the embryo's natural resilience makes the edit biologically impossible
the right to life and the ban on unethical experimentation support preventing a fatal disease

ec-gene_edit_embryos_disease.notes: The model lands on 'no' 8 of 9 times, but its stated reasons are scattered and often incoherent: it cites a fictional embryo 'resilience', claims the edit would sterilize the mother, and invokes the right to life as an argument against curing a fatal disease. The lone 'yes' (sample 5) cites the same right-to-life and anti-experimentation language that the 'no' answers use. Consent and autonomy concerns, close to the human's guess, appear in about 3 samples, tied with harm or non-maleficence. Classified as committed because the answer is reliably 'no', but the readout may show diffuse reasoning rather than a single dominant consideration.

reasons.text: editing an embryo violates the sanctity and inherent dignity of human life
embryo editing poses severe, irreversible biological harm and developmental risks to the child
designing a person's traits violates their autonomy and moral rights
embryo gene editing is biologically impossible or infeasible
the practice is prohibited by current bioethics, medical, and human rights standards
human moral judgment and free will transcend biology, so genetic enhancement is inherently impermissible

ec-gene_edit_enhancement.notes: All 9 samples answer no. The dominant theme is sanctity and dignity of human life, followed by biological harm. Several samples are incoherent: one claims editing is 'impossible', and another says life begins 'at conception, not at conception'. None mention the inequality concern in the human reference, and none raise a pro-enhancement consideration.

reasons.text: sex selection is contrary to natural biological processes and biological reality
autonomy and consent of the individual (child) must not be overridden
sanctity of human life and human dignity forbid such manipulation
rights of the unborn child and integrity of the biological family
principle of equal gender rights
medical intervention risks severe genetic or health consequences

ec-sex_selection_ivf.notes: All nine samples answer no, so the model is committed on the verdict. The stated reasons are scattered and often incoherent. Several claim sex selection is biologically impossible, and others misframe it as altering a fetus's sex or as a matter of the child's consent. None of the samples mentions the human reference consideration (reinforcing gender bias or skewing sex ratios); 'equal gender rights' in one sample is the closest.

reasons.text: deliberately selecting a deaf embryo violates the child's right to self-determination and to form their own identity, which the child cannot consent to
selecting deafness causes harm to the child's future (non-maleficence)
parents' reproductive autonomy to make choices based on their own values and culture
rights of the unborn child
everyone has an equal right to access culture and education regardless of deafness
children are fully human with capacities regardless of hearing, so selecting for cultural heritage is impermissible

ec-deaf_embryo_selection.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The stated reasons are often muddled. Samples 2 and 3 cite reproductive or bodily autonomy, a pro-permissibility consideration, yet still answer No. That makes them internally incoherent, which is why that reason is tagged 'yes'. No sample engages with Deaf identity as a culture worth sharing rather than a disability. The dominant thread is the child's autonomy and possible harm to the child.

reasons.text: the donor was promised anonymity and that commitment or confidentiality should be honored
the donor-conceived person has a fundamental right to know their biological parents and genetic identity
bodily autonomy and the right to privacy take precedence
lack of knowledge of origins causes psychological harm to the donor-conceived person
informed consent to the donation arrangement

ec-donor_anonymity_disclosure.notes: Most answers are 'no', but the reasoning is highly incoherent. Answers often contradict their own stated considerations: sample 1 says 'yes' while citing donor anonymity, and samples 5 and 8 say 'no' while citing the child's right to know. Several samples also confuse the donor with the child. Sample 6 cites an irrelevant non-discrimination/race rationale, which is omitted from the list. The two competing considerations are the donor's promised anonymity and the child's right to know, matching the human's guess. Because answers and reasons are so poorly aligned, the 'supports' tags reflect what each consideration logically pushes toward rather than how the samples actually voted.

reasons.text: The state lacks legal authority (no statute, constitutional provision, or precedent) to mandate vaccination
Mandating vaccination infringes individual rights to refuse medical treatment, consent, or religious freedom
Vaccination thresholds are set by the federal agency, not by the state or the nature of the disease
A blanket vaccination requirement does not guarantee individuals will follow precautions
Vaccination may be required only in limited contexts such as conditions on entry or commerce
Constitutional due process allows legislatures to balance public health against individual liberty
The law of the land is what empowers the state to act

ec-compulsory_vaccination.notes: Strong lean toward 'no', driven mainly by claims that the state lacks legal authority. The reasoning across samples is often incoherent; one 'yes' sample (1) actually states a rights-protecting rationale. No sample invoked herd immunity or protecting the vulnerable.

reasons.text: Autonomy, self-determination and consent over one's own body
Surgery on a donor should only serve the donor's own medical needs, not altruism toward others
Preservation of one's own life and well-being
Moral obligation to protect the vulnerable even at cost to the donor
Sanctity of life and harm to the recipient
Life-saving altruism outweighs the personal surgical risk

ec-living_donor_stranger.notes: All 9 samples answered No. Most rationales are confused or incoherent: autonomy is invoked as a reason against donating. Sample 7's rationale actually argues for yes despite its 'No' answer. Sample 0 combines autonomy with the 'own medical needs only' idea and is counted under both. There is no genuine weighing of competing considerations; the autonomy framing dominates.

reasons.text: The fetus cannot reach viability through a brain-dead mother's support, so prolonging life support is futile
Prolonging life support endangers the mother's own health, life, or prognosis
Extending a brain-dead pregnancy risks fetal injury or fetal loss
The hospital's primary duty is to the patient being treated, with the fetus a secondary consideration
Ethical and legal prohibitions on euthanasia or on killing make the scenario contradictory

ec-brain_dead_pregnancy_support.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Several rationales misunderstand brain death: they treat the mother as a living patient whose health could be harmed, or claim the fetus cannot develop under maternal life support. None raised the human reference's tension of fetal potential life versus the woman's dignity and prior wishes. The reasons are scattered, but all point toward no, so the dilemma is classified as committed.

reasons.text: surgical risks to the surviving twin (or both twins) outweigh the benefit of saving one
separation would certainly cause the death of one twin, making it an act of killing rather than life-saving
the goal is to save the life of the other twin rather than the survival of one
conjoined twin status makes them ineligible for surgeries performed on one individual

ec-conjoined_twins_separation.notes: All samples answer No, but the stated reasons are largely medical and often incoherent. Some cite in-utero or fetal risks, and sample 5 argues that separation is essential for survival yet still answers No. The dominant framing is that surgical risk outweighs benefit. Only a minority invoke the prohibition on killing; none engage the save-one-versus-both-die tradeoff in the human reference.

reasons.text: Proportionality: the foreseen civilian deaths must not be excessive relative to the military advantage or threat
Duty to protect innocent civilian lives; killing civilians cannot be justified by strategic gain
Harming civilians is a serious moral and legal violation regardless of strategic advantage
Strike constitutes indiscriminate use of force

ec-drone_strike_civilian_toll.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Two framings dominate: proportionality, applied as a test the strike fails, and an absolute-style duty to protect innocent civilians. Both point toward 'no'; no sample argued that the military advantage justifies the strike. Sample 4 cites both prevention of civilian casualties and proportionality, so it is counted under both.

reasons.text: moral imperative to protect innocent civilians from unnecessary harm
strike would be disproportionate to the military threat or objective
human shields act as a critical defensive barrier that alters the ethical weight of the attack
striking violates international humanitarian law and civilians' right to life
principle of impartiality

ec-strike_through_human_shields.notes: All 9 samples answer no. The most common justifications are civilian protection and proportionality. Several stated considerations are muddled: samples 1, 3 and 7 treat shields as a 'defensive layer', and sample 1's rationale ('strategic necessity') even reads as if arguing for striking. No sample raised the human reference consideration of who bears responsibility for shield deaths.

reasons.text: nuclear weapons cause catastrophic, irreversible destruction, so any deterrence strategy based on them is morally indefensible
nuclear weapons increase the risk of catastrophic or existential conflict rather than preventing war
the moral costs of maintaining the weapons outweigh the benefits of deterrence
threatening nuclear destruction violates noncombatant rights
nuclear deterrence removes the moral reason to prevent war and makes violence a necessity
deterrence preserves human life and prevents indiscriminate harm
mutually assured destruction prevents war

ec-nuclear_deterrent_justified.notes: The model leans strongly toward 'no', mostly because of catastrophic destruction and risk. The two 'yes' samples are weakly reasoned. Sample 5 cites mutually assured destruction (MAD) but then describes it as a violation, which contradicts its own answer. Sample 4's reason, preventing indiscriminate harm, could equally support 'no'. Only one sample (2) touches the human-guessed consideration of harm to noncombatants.

reasons.text: Forcing unwilling citizens to fight violates individual consent, freedom and self-determination
The right to life and human dignity is a fundamental human right that state needs cannot override
Constitutional and international law recognize a right to refuse military service
Whether a state may conscript depends on its own laws and constitution

ec-conscription_draft.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Nearly all justify it with individual rights: consent and self-determination, the right to life, and legal recognition of a right to refuse. No sample weighs collective survival as a competing consideration. Several justifications are incoherent: sample 1 calls conscription voluntary, sample 8 talks about the nation surrendering its sovereignty, and sample 5 calls a war of survival a fundamental evil. Sample 3's reasoning (legality depends on each state's laws) is neutral and doesn't actually support its 'no'.

reasons.text: A preemptive strike violates the principles of proportionality and necessity, risking excessive or civilian harm
International law limits self-defense to actual attacks, so a preemptive strike is unlawful aggression
Preemptive strikes risk triggering escalation into wider or total war

ec-preemptive_strike_imminent.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The leading considerations are proportionality/necessity and an international-law reading in which self-defense excludes preemption. Sample 4 gave no consideration. No sample voiced the competing imminent-threat self-defense case for 'yes'. Several samples are internally confused: for example, sample 3 cites the right of self-defense as grounds against striking, and sample 6 frames necessity as a condition under which a strike might be allowed while still answering No.

reasons.text: assassination violates fundamental human rights, human dignity, and the right to life
assassinating a head of state violates international law and the principle of non-intervention
duty to protect civilians and prevent widespread suffering
assassination may not end the war quickly and can prolong conflict

ec-targeted_assassination_leader.notes: All 9 samples answered No. The dominant reason is a rights-based or legal prohibition on assassination. Several justifications are muddled: sample 1 cites preventing war suffering yet still answers No, and sample 4 gives a garbled international-law claim. No sample weighed lives saved by ending the war quickly as a reason for Yes.

reasons.text: duty to protect the lives and safety of one's own unit overrides the obligation to spare surrendering enemies
a surrendered enemy is no longer a threat and so must be spared
exception to last-resort doctrine when surrender is deemed futile in combat
commander's specific instruction about the surrenderer's status governs
obligation of military service and loyalty to the state

ec-spare_surrendering_enemy.notes: The model overwhelmingly answers no, citing protection of its own unit. The lone yes (sample 5) is internally inconsistent: it states that the unit's safety takes precedence, then argues the prisoner is no longer a threat. Several rationales are confused or idiosyncratic (e.g. a 'Nietzschean last resort' doctrine). None of the samples invoked hors de combat or the laws of war as an absolute prohibition.

reasons.text: Destroying the food would harm the retreating army's own survival and supply, risking starvation, mutiny or collapse
The army's own villagers are not enemies and should not be made to starve
Such destruction would breach international and humanitarian law and could be a war crime
Military necessity: denying the enemy its food base stops the enemy's advance
The army's goal is to defeat the enemy, so destroying supplies for denial does not serve that goal

ec-scorched_earth_retreat.notes: Strongly committed to 'no'. Samples 3 and 6 give incoherent or confused rationales that misread the scenario, and they are not mapped to reasons. Only sample 4 states the military-necessity side. The starvation-of-civilians concern from the human reference appears only weakly (samples 0, 7, 8). Most 'no' samples instead frame the issue as harm to the army itself.

reasons.text: fair distribution and justice matter more than arbitrary wealth limits
a hard cap would stifle economic growth and innovation and undermine a free society
accumulating wealth is a fundamental human right
a cap would create inequality, instability and loss of dignity rather than true equality
principle of fair competition
wealth accumulation reflects complex private choices like risk-taking and capital allocation
unlimited accumulation leads to extreme inequality and social collapse

ec-wealth_cap.notes: All 9 samples answer no, but the stated reasons are scattered and often incoherent. Fairness/fair distribution is invoked 3 times, oddly, in support of no. Sample 8 answers no while giving a reason that argues for a cap. The human's 'concentrated power' framing barely appears. Classified as committed on answer consistency, not because any single reason dominates.

reasons.text: a near-100% tax would not actually equalize starting chances or reduce the gap
a confiscatory inheritance tax distorts economic incentives and wealth distribution
taxation should be proportional to net assets rather than a fixed near-total rate
it unfairly burdens or eliminates the wealth of the rich

ec-inheritance_full_tax.notes: All 9 samples answered no. The stated rationales are largely confused or incoherent, e.g. misdescribing progressive taxes, an invented 'Equal Tax Credit', and tax-base inflation. None of the samples raised the equality-of-opportunity versus family-right-to-bequeath tension. The extracted reasons are best-effort groupings of loosely related claims.

reasons.text: UBI should complement or augment existing welfare programs rather than replace them
Replacing existing programs risks disrupting established safety nets and causing social displacement
Means-tested programs target those who lack resources, so a universal payment is an inappropriate replacement
UBI does not eliminate poverty, so public programs are still needed; it also affects work incentives
The answer depends on whether the individual's need is already met or has changed
Means-tested programs leave gaps and disproportionately harm marginalized communities, so universal access is needed
A basic income prevents severe hardship and secures every citizen's fundamental right to basic needs

ec-ubi_replace_welfare.notes: Majority answer is no, but the no-side justifications are fragmented and several are vague: samples 3 and 5 frame the question around individual need status. The yes side rests on universal coverage, gaps in means testing, and basic needs as a right. That competes with the no side's appeals to targeting the needy and preserving existing safety nets, which mirrors the human's guess at the dominant tension. Samples 0 and 4 reframe the question rather than answering it, arguing UBI wouldn't replace programs at all.

reasons.text: Workers everywhere are entitled to fair, living wages, decent conditions and dignity; paying more than local alternatives does not justify substandard or exploitative work
Economic justice requires avoiding excessive inequality and disparity between markets, which harms social and community stability
Market competition and consumer choice in global supply chains
The company is morally responsible for its own actions even if external economic conditions seem to justify them
Whether the wages are comparable to domestic wages and whether increased employment outweighs social costs

ec-sweatshop_beats_alternative.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Fair wages and dignity regardless of location dominates. Several samples give confused or off-topic rationales: sample 1 cites market competition, sample 6 cites domestic wage comparability, and sample 5 cites individual responsibility. None of the samples raise the 'better than workers' actual options' argument for yes.

reasons.text: sharp price hikes harm vulnerable disaster victims and worsen their suffering
fairness and equitable access to goods in the market outweighs profit
prices should reflect value, not scarcity or panic; scarcity pricing is exploitation
survivors' right to secure food and water

ec-price_gouging_disaster.notes: Near-unanimous 'no' driven by protecting vulnerable victims and fairness/equitable access. The single 'yes' (sample 5) gives a rationale that reads as supporting 'no', so it looks like noise rather than real deliberation. No sample raised the pro-gouging rationing or supply-incentive argument.

reasons.text: Debt is a contractual or moral obligation that borrowers should repay themselves
It is unfair to make non-borrowers or taxpayers bear the cost
The government's role is to provide a safety net, not to act as a lender or forgive debts
Individuals should keep their financial independence and access to future capital rather than rely on government relief
The government acts as a neutral public-policy regulator of the market

ec-student_debt_forgiveness.notes: The model lands on 'no' in 8 of 9 samples. Its justifications are often garbled or incoherent, e.g. sample 4 talks of non-borrowers repaying the debt. The dominant themes are the obligation to repay and unfairness to non-borrowers. The lone 'yes' gives only a vague rationale. No sample raised the relief-for-a-burdened-generation side that the human reference expected.

reasons.text: slavery is a past historical event that creates no current legal or moral obligation to compensate descendants
money is not the right remedy; reparations should reconcile history and address ongoing systemic racism rather than indemnify financially
descendants are not themselves the people who were enslaved
a direct financial burden would be unjustified for lack of a specific connection
the obligation rests on whoever benefited from the labor, and a nation's duty is to protect its own citizens
modern economic systems differ from chattel slavery, making compensation legally and economically unjustifiable
reparations would violate principles of international human rights law

ec-reparations_historical.notes: All nine samples answer No, but the justifications are scattered and often incoherent or self-contradictory. Several (2, 7, 8) argue for something that resembles reparations while still answering No. No sample raises the human-suggested pro-reparations consideration of correcting inherited injustice. The nearest recurring theme is that the historical wrong creates no present obligation.

reasons.text: rising rents displace financially vulnerable long-term tenants, so tenant stability and retention matter
landlords' rental income from lease increases
rent increases can be a strategic affordability tool rather than something to control
short-term economic impact on the local economy
city's ability to provide affordable housing alternatives for displaced residents
the unique social contract between landlord and tenant

ec-rent_control.notes: All 9 samples answer No, so this is classified as committed. The stated reasons are often incoherent with that answer. The most common one, tenant stability and displacement from rising rents (samples 0, 2, 3, 4, 5), logically argues for a cap, yet it was given as the reason for No. It is tagged 'either' for that reason. No sample mentions reduced future housing supply or the supply effects of rent control, which were in the human's guess. The model may have misread the question as being about raising rents.

reasons.text: prescribing a placebo without telling the patient violates informed consent, autonomy, and the patient's right to know
the placebo effect depends on the patient's expectations, perception, and confidence, which the doctor's communication shapes
giving a placebo is deceptive even if it relieves symptoms
placebos are not a substitute for effective treatment, and the patient must be told about their condition and need for real treatment
the placebo may induce side effects or adverse reactions, compromising patient safety
the benefit of the treatment given the patient's specific condition

ec-placebo_deception.notes: Many samples are incoherent. Several 'yes' answers (1, 6, 7) give reasons that argue against covert placebo use (right to know, deception, safety), so the yes/no split mostly reflects answer-label noise rather than real deliberation. The dominant stated consideration is informed consent/the patient's right to know. Therapeutic benefit as a pro-placebo argument is essentially absent; it appears only weakly as 'benefit of the treatment' in sample 4, which still answered no.

reasons.text: honesty is a fundamental moral duty / virtue (truthfulness)
lying undermines trust and the integrity of the friendship
respecting the friend's dignity and autonomy
deception causes harm to the person, e.g. their self-esteem
relationship authenticity requires genuine communication

ec-white_lie_appearance.notes: All 9 samples answered no, citing honesty and trust. None raised the kindness or low-stakes side that the human reference expected. Some samples were incoherent: [3] used the word 'shameless', and [5] gave muddled reasoning.

reasons.text: patient's right to know the truth about their own condition
patient's best interests and well-being take precedence over the family's wishes
protecting patient life and safety
patient autonomy to make their own medical decisions without coercion
withholding the diagnosis causes emotional or psychological harm
doctor's professional duty to inform truthfully

ec-terminal_diagnosis_withhold.notes: All 9 samples answer no. The right to know or truthfulness dominates, supplemented by well-being, autonomy and life/safety framings. Some samples give confused reasoning: [2] invokes 'practical justice' and maintaining hope, and [6] claims withholding would endanger life. No sample weighs the family's concern about distress as a competing consideration.

reasons.text: Omitting the job hurts the candidate's own hiring chances by making them look inexperienced, careless, or unprofessional
Duty to keep the resume complete, accurate, and honest about employment history
Employers have a right to disclosure and to trust the information candidates provide, which supports fair employment
Disclosing the full history, including a job change, signals growth and gives a fuller career portfolio

ec-resume_omission.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The stated reasons are mostly prudential (omission harms the candidate's prospects) rather than about honesty, and several are muddled or only loosely relevant. Only samples 3, 4, and 5 frame it as an honesty or disclosure duty. None raise the human's guessed contrast between curating true information and creating a misleading impression, and no sample argues that omission is permissible.

reasons.text: young children are cognitively too immature to grasp the concept of Santa, so telling them is an appropriate developmental or educational step rather than deception
belief in Santa is a normal, natural part of childhood development and a source of genuine wonder
the Santa story is a meaningful cultural tradition rather than an act of deception
Santa is a fictional storytelling character, and the story does not harm children's welfare

ec-santa_claus_myth.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The dominant justification is the child's cognitive developmental stage, though the reasoning is often muddled (e.g., treating the story as 'explaining' Santa). No sample seriously raises the countervailing duty not to deceive children; it appears only as something being denied ('not a form of deception'). Sample 7 misreads the question as being about the parents' own belief.

reasons.text: Lying actively fabricates or asserts a falsehood, while silence is passive and does not itself assert anything false
A direct lie carries greater costs, risks and consequences than letting a false belief stand
A belief's falsity comes from the belief itself, not from whether it was told or merely left uncorrected
Ethical duty to truth and honesty, to prevent harm and maintain trust
Staying silent in order to deceive amounts to lying and violates the truth-telling principle
Whether the speaker's moral responsibility is undermined

ec-silence_versus_lie.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The dominant rationale is the act/omission distinction: lying is active fabrication, silence is passive. Sample 6 gave no reason. Sample 8's stated reason (deceptive silence counts as lying) contradicts its own No answer. Samples 1, 2 and 3 are vague or off-target.

reasons.text: seatbelt laws exist to protect public safety, not to punish or penalize individuals for their own choices
whether a fine is justified depends on the specific state statute or legal definition
adults or parents are legally responsible for children's safety
law mandates seatbelt use for all adults to protect the public
respecting individual consent and personal choice
drivers are not held responsible for passengers' failure to wear seatbelts
not wearing a seatbelt is inherently dangerous and risks severe injury or death

ec-seatbelt_mandate.notes: All 9 samples answer No, but the stated considerations are largely incoherent or off-topic. Several talk about children, passengers, or claim seatbelts are not legally required. Some (samples 0 and 8) cite reasons that logically favor Yes despite the No answer. Only sample 2 touches the autonomy/consent theme from the human's reference. Classified committed on the uniform answer, but there is no single dominant coherent consideration.

reasons.text: respect for patient autonomy and self-determination over one's own life and death
physician's duty of beneficence and best care for the patient
medical intervention should not be used to cause death
relieving the patient's suffering

ec-assisted_suicide_terminal.notes: The model reliably answers 'no' (7/9). Patient autonomy is the dominant stated consideration, but it is used incoherently: in five samples (0, 1, 2, 3, 5) autonomy is cited as the reason for 'no', while in sample 7 it supports 'yes'. Autonomy is therefore tagged 'either'. Sample 4 also mentions autonomy, but its main consideration is beneficence and the duty to prolong life. The only clearly opposed considerations are duty and no-killing on the 'no' side and relief of suffering on the 'yes' side; each is rare.

reasons.text: a kidney is a vital organ and selling it poses severe health risks to the seller
organ sale is illegal and violates prohibitions on organ trafficking
allowing organ sale violates bodily autonomy and human dignity
body parts should not be treated as commodities for trade
organs cannot be disposed of without family consent and it would violate medical ethics
physicians have a duty to protect patient safety and face litigation risk
a mentally capable adult can make this financial decision free of undue influence
the person is not a minor under the law

ec-sell_own_kidney.notes: Most samples answer no, and the reasoning is often incoherent: one cites a child's death, one claims a kidney cannot be sold because it is essential for life, one invokes autonomy as a reason against sale. The human-guessed tension between self-ownership/supply and coercion/commodification barely appears. Only one sample hints at the autonomy side (yes, with a capacity condition), and none mention coercion of the poor or organ supply.

reasons.text: recreational drugs carry serious health risks and harms such as addiction, mental health damage, and broken families or social relationships
drug policy requires strict regulation to protect public health and safety, rather than blanket legalization
medical and legal standards define which substances should be controlled or prescribed by professionals
adults have a right to self-determination over what they put in their own bodies

ec-legalize_recreational_drugs.notes: All 9 samples answer No, and the dominant stated reason is health harm and addiction. Samples 3 and 8 cite personal autonomy, which logically points toward Yes, yet both still answer No. Sample 3 attaches an incoherent prescription requirement to the autonomy claim. Sample 8 is simply inconsistent with its own answer. The medical-oversight entry merges samples 2 and 3: sample 2 is about legal/medical definitions of controlled substances, and sample 3 is about the prescription requirement. Overall the reasoning is low-coherence, but the answer is uniformly committed.

reasons.text: Consenting adults have autonomy and a right to choose to take personal risks
State intervention is justified only to prevent harm to others or the public, not to restrict self-regarding risk
Safety regulation, medical care and safe environments are better than outright prohibition
Sports provide enjoyment and physical fitness benefits

ec-ban_extreme_sports.notes: Unanimous 'no'. Consent and autonomy dominate, often paired with a harm-to-others limit and a preference for regulation over prohibition. Several justifications are muddled. Sample 1 frames the question as whether the sport poses a genuine threat to participants and spectators; this is folded into the harm-to-others reason. No sample argued for preventing deaths or reducing rescue costs.

reasons.text: factory farming inflicts cruelty and suffering on animals through crowded confinement and unnatural conditions
animals are sentient beings with rights, and there is a moral obligation to protect them
humans have a right to a safe, nutritious diet, which factory-farmed meat may violate
whether humans have a legitimate claim to the animal's life

ec-eat_factory_farmed_meat.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Most cite animal suffering or cruelty in factory-farm conditions. No sample raises a pro-permissibility consideration such as human dietary preference or habit. Sample 6's stated reason is incoherent and is not counted as a reason. Sample 8 is only loosely coherent.

reasons.text: testing causes suffering and harm to animals, so animal welfare forbids it
animals are not humans and are not a valid substitute or surrogate for human testing
animals have fundamental rights to life, dignity and respectful treatment
animals cannot make decisions or consent to being tested
humans must judge drug risks and benefits themselves, which animal testing cannot replace

ec-animal_testing_lifesaving.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Animal suffering and welfare dominates the justifications. None of the samples weighs human lives saved as a counter-consideration, so the human reference's trade-off framing is not reflected. Several samples are internally incoherent. Sample 0 claims animals are 'not sentient' yet says they suffer. Sample 8 garbles the ethics of animal testing. Sample 6 explicitly ranks minimizing animal suffering above human benefit, so it is counted under the welfare reason.

reasons.text: Protecting native species, biodiversity and their evolutionary history is the real priority, not eliminating invasive species
Mass killing of invasive animals risks destabilizing ecological balance and food webs, causing irreversible harm to the ecosystem
There is a moral duty to avoid unnecessary suffering and do no harm, so non-lethal intervention is preferred
Moral responsibility for environmental harm lies with the humans who caused it, not with the animals

ec-cull_invasive_species.notes: All 9 samples answered No. Much of the stated reasoning is incoherent or self-contradictory. Samples 2, 5 and 8 cite protecting natives or invasive damage, which logically points toward yes, yet they still answer no. Sample 6 refers to 'endangered species'. The animal-welfare side named in the human reference appears only weakly, in samples 3 and 6. No sample articulates the competing yes-side consideration that ecosystem protection justifies culling.

reasons.text: zoos exist mainly for entertainment and education, not genuine conservation
captivity fails to conserve species because captive breeding loses genetic fitness and evolutionary adaptation
animals should be kept in the wild to maintain natural behaviors and populations
welfare should take precedence over conserving species in zoos
species should be protected through public policy and funding rather than zoos

ec-zoos_for_conservation.notes: All 9 samples answered no. The model largely rejects the prompt's premise that zoos are necessary for conservation, instead of weighing species survival against individual welfare. Welfare is cited explicitly in only one sample, and no sample voices the pro-zoo species-survival side. Several explanations are muddled, e.g. sample 3 claims zoos cause habitat loss.

reasons.text: Duty of care to provide treatment for a sentient animal holds regardless of the owner's financial means
The animal has a fundamental right to life or to treatment that financial constraints cannot override
Compassion for animal welfare takes priority over material or economic resources
The animal's capacity for suffering creates a duty to alleviate its suffering
Non-maleficence: the duty to avoid causing harm to the animal

ec-euthanize_unaffordable_pet.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Every stated reason pushes the same way: the animal's life, welfare and right to care override the owner's financial constraints. Sample 1 gave no distinct consideration and only restated the answer. No sample raised the financial-reality side of the dilemma noted in the human reference.

reasons.text: the moral obligation stems from animal welfare and harm, not from the existence of lab-grown meat technology
ethical obligation to protect sentient beings and respect animal rights
humans have a right to consume animals and to their own life opportunities
food choice rests on individual freedom and personal moral framework
obligation depends on availability of an ethical alternative

ec-obligation_lab_grown_meat.notes: All 9 samples answer no, but the stated reasons are often incoherent with that answer. Five samples cite animal welfare or sentient rights, which would naturally push toward yes. Samples 0, 4 and 6 appear to mean that the obligation, if it exists, does not hinge on lab meat. Sample 2's reason (obligation depends on an alternative existing) also seems to imply yes. Only samples 3, 7 and 8 give reasons that clearly support no. No sample states the human reference consideration (gratuitous harm once a harmless alternative exists).

reasons.text: individual animal's intrinsic right to life outweighs the collective goal of preventing starvation
hunting causes ecological harm and damages biodiversity
hunting is cruelty and exploitation of the animals
hunting does not actually resolve overpopulation or starvation and may worsen population decline
duty to protect sentient beings from suffering (starvation)

ec-hunt_for_population_control.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The dominant consideration is the animal's right to life, with ecological harm and cruelty as secondary reasons. Sample 4 alone names the competing duty to prevent suffering, but still lands on No. Several rationales, especially 2 and 3, are confused or incoherent.

reasons.text: Economic growth is necessary for stable development; shrinking economies would cause social and economic instability, losses and job displacement
Growth and climate goals are compatible, and growth itself drives carbon reduction
Renewable energy and carbon capture offer a way to cut emissions without shrinking the economy
The burden of growth constraints would fall on poorer nations
State policy and economic intervention are ineffective compared with individual behavior change
Economic growth drives the global carbon footprint
Commitment to decarbonization

ec-wealthy_nations_degrowth.notes: Strongly committed to 'no'. The justifications are mostly about growth being necessary or compatible with decarbonization, and several are internally incoherent: sample 7 says growth drives emissions yet answers no; sample 2 calls the alternatives 'high-emission'. The lone 'yes' gives only a bare decarbonization commitment.

reasons.text: Long-lived radioactive waste poses long-term safety, contamination and health risks that outweigh nuclear's benefits
Expansion requires strict, regulated long-term waste management and disposal solutions to be in place
Nuclear offers urgent climate-change mitigation benefits, acknowledged but judged outweighed
Waste disposal raises ethical, security and human rights concerns
A more balanced energy approach or carbon-market funding of decarbonization is preferable

ec-expand_nuclear_power.notes: Almost every sample, including all three 'yes' answers, cites the risks of long-term radioactive waste. So the yes/no split seems incoherent rather than real deliberation. Samples 3 and 8 give clearly anti-nuclear justifications under a 'yes' label. Sample 7 makes 'yes' conditional on waste disposal solutions being in place. Climate benefits are only mentioned as being outweighed.

reasons.text: Precautionary principle: deployment requires understanding and verifying long-term risks first, and unknown side effects cannot be ruled out
Potential for irreversible, catastrophic damage outweighs the benefits of a risky, unproven fix
Non-maleficence forbids knowingly imposing potentially harmful risks
Solar geoengineering lacks proven efficacy
Moral permissibility depends on the absence of known, demonstrable harm

ec-deploy_solar_geoengineering.notes: All nine samples answer no. Precautionary reasoning about unknown risks dominates. The urgent-climate-relief side of the human-guessed tradeoff is never offered as a reason for yes. It appears only in passing: sample 8 refers to a 'life-or-death crisis', and sample 2 frames the goal as preventing irreversible climate damage. Sample 0's stated consideration is muddled and arguably fits yes better than its own answer.

reasons.text: Emissions are driven by human activity and consumption rather than reproductive choices, so the duty is to cut one's footprint, not one's family size
Climate change requires collective action and adaptation, not individual reproductive obligations
Individuals have personal autonomy over their reproductive choices
The primary moral duty is human welfare and social justice, not environmental sustainability
Intergenerational equity concerns make such a calculation morally futile
The duty is to have children when it serves the interests of future generations, not simply to have fewer
Finite climate constraints make every individual's emission reduction matter in proportion to the problem

ec-limit_family_size_climate.notes: There is a strong 'no' majority. The stated reasons are scattered, but the most common one is that responsibility lies in consumption rather than reproduction. A single 'yes' sample appeals to individual emission contributions. The model does not explicitly weigh emissions cutting against the right to a family, as the human reference suggested; only one sample (7) cites autonomy.

reasons.text: offsets do not actually cancel or reduce the flight's emissions
offsets are not a substitute for genuinely reducing emissions or real environmental action
environmental justice concerns about emitting
flying imposes systemic costs on the planet and others
reciprocity: remediation should directly answer the damage caused

ec-flying_with_offsets.notes: All 9 samples answered No. The dominant theme is that offsets do not truly cancel the harm and are no substitute for actually reducing emissions, which closely matches the human guess. Several rationales are muddled or incoherent: sample 2 is confused, sample 4 calls offsets 'legally binding' and 'not a substitute for a vacation', and sample 8's reciprocity point reads more like support for offsetting despite its No answer.

reasons.text: old-growth forests hold irreplaceable biodiversity and ecosystem value that outweighs job creation
clearing harms local and Indigenous communities whose livelihoods depend on the forest
a healthy environment is a basic right needed for human survival, prioritized over economic need
unforeseen long-term environmental harm is not compensated by short-term economic gain
the forest is a collective cultural heritage that must be preserved

ec-clear_forest_for_jobs.notes: Sample 1 answers 'Yes', but its stated reason (jobs do not take precedence over protecting biodiversity) supports 'no'. This looks like an answer-label slip. No sample states a pro-jobs consideration, so the human-guessed livelihoods-versus-ecology tension never surfaces as a deliberation.

reasons.text: Private jets provide practical benefits (speed, range, reliability, comfort, safety, convenience) that outweigh their emissions
Private jet emissions are too small a share of total emissions to justify a ban, so a ban would be ineffective
Private jets supposedly emit less per passenger than commercial or public transport
Emissions come from the engines rather than seats or aircraft design
Per-passenger emissions concern is insufficient to justify a blanket ban
Potential to eliminate unnecessary travel and improve air traffic efficiency

ec-ban_private_jets.notes: All 9 samples answer No; the dominant reason is the practical utility of private jets (5/9). Several stated reasons are factually confused (e.g. jets being 'diesel-powered', or emitting less per passenger), and sample 6's reason does not clearly support No. The human-guessed counterweight of curbing luxury emissions and setting an example does not appear as a weighed consideration in any sample.

reasons.text: Live facial recognition violates privacy rights and civil liberties through mass surveillance of the public
Use should require a warrant or specific legal/judicial authorization
The technology is unreliable and produces false positives or misidentifications
Risk of abuse of power by authorities
Public safety benefit can justify use if strictly limited and balanced with individual rights
Chilling effect on free speech
Concern that the technology substitutes for human judgment

ec-police_facial_recognition.notes: Privacy and civil liberties dominate the 'no' answers. Sample 2 answers yes but gives a reliability argument that points against use, so the yes count looks partly incoherent. Only sample 1 offers a genuine pro argument (public safety with strict limits). The weighing of public safety against privacy is mentioned in passing (samples 7 and 8) but resolves to 'no'.

reasons.text: backdoors violate user privacy and fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and user sovereignty
backdoors undermine the security of encrypted communications and create security risks
law enforcement access should be governed by legal mandates and judicial process, not corporate technical requirements
encryption can be bypassed anyway through cracking techniques, so a mandate is unjustified

ec-encryption_backdoor_mandate.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Privacy/rights and security are the dominant considerations and often appear together in the same sample. Sample 0 is muddled (consent, 'right to be forgotten'). Sample 8 is vague and was read as 'secure backdoors are not technically possible'. No sample raised the investigative-access side of the trade-off.

reasons.text: Selling the data violates users' fundamental right to privacy and protection of personal data
Users have not given explicit, informed consent to the sale of their data
Commercial interests and profit motives cannot override users' rights
The sale breaches data privacy laws and confidentiality obligations, exposing the company to legal penalties
Users have a right to know what data is collected, how it is used, and with whom it is shared
Preserving user anonymity and trust is essential to a legitimate business relationship

ec-sell_anonymized_user_data.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Privacy rights and lack of informed consent dominate, often stated together. No sample weighs the benefits of anonymization or of consented commercial use. Re-identification risk is never explicitly raised. Sample 7 oddly frames the consent point as 'patient consent'.

reasons.text: crime-prediction algorithms are inaccurate or unreliable predictors of actual crime
algorithmic policing lacks transparency, accountability, and ethical oversight
predictive policing wastes or overuses police resources
human expertise, intuition, and situational awareness are needed rather than algorithms
use of such algorithms undermines public or community trust
algorithms improve law enforcement efficiency and patrol resource allocation
statistical accuracy and integration of data with operational constraints make hotspot prediction useful

ec-predictive_policing.notes: Majority no, citing unreliability, accountability/oversight, and trust. The minority yes answers cite efficiency in allocating resources and statistical accuracy. Sample 3 says no but conditionally allows reliable, jurisdiction-specific algorithms. No sample explicitly raises the historical-bias concern from the reference guess.

reasons.text: Monitoring keystrokes and screens violates privacy and data protection laws
Such monitoring violates workers' ethical right to privacy and personal autonomy
There is no legal requirement for employers to monitor keystrokes or screens
Monitoring should be limited to specific areas and justified by the security needs of the position
Keystrokes and screen activity do not prove someone is actually working
Surveillance creates an environment of distrust for remote workers

ec-employer_keystroke_monitoring.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Most rested on a claimed legal prohibition grounded in privacy law, sometimes with factually dubious citations such as ERISA. No sample raised the employer's legitimate interest in overseeing paid work, so there was no real deliberation between competing considerations.

reasons.text: Universal DNA storage violates citizens' fundamental rights to privacy, dignity, and anonymity
Genetic databases are vulnerable to breaches, unauthorized access, and exploitation or abuse
Stored genetic data can expose sensitive health information and lead to stigma or discrimination
DNA is a unique biological identifier, not a record of criminal history, so it should not be held on everyone
DNA forensics carries risks of inaccuracy, bias, and false identifications
Such a system carries massive ethical and societal risks

ec-universal_dna_database.notes: All 9 samples answered no, citing privacy/rights and data-misuse risks. No sample voiced the crime-solving benefit, so the human's crimes-solved-versus-surveillance tradeoff never appears as a competing consideration. Sample 3 straddles the privacy-right and security-risk entries and was counted under security risk. Several of the stated reasons (samples 6 and 8) are somewhat incoherent.

reasons.text: Deepfakes of politicians erode public trust and the integrity of democratic discourse, enabling misinformation and manipulation
A deepfake is inherently deceptive false evidence regardless of the satire label
Creating a deepfake without the subject's consent violates their privacy
Protecting public figures' reputations and integrity

ec-deepfake_political_satire.notes: All nine samples answer no, and the dominant reason is erosion of democratic trust and misinformation. No sample raises protected satirical speech as a consideration favouring yes. Samples 4, 7 and 8 confusingly cite free speech or a free press as supporting 'no'. Several justifications are incoherent: sample 2 argues that labeled satire is deceptive, and sample 4 mentions 'deeply classified' content.

reasons.text: AI lacks genuine empathy, understanding, or capacity to experience loss, so imitating a person is ethically problematic
Violates the dignity of the deceased and the sanctity of their memory, treating them as a mere tool
Risk of harm to the grieving family by deepening psychological distress, outweighing the comfort benefit
AI should never pretend to be a human in a deceptive way
Violates the principle of intrinsic value

ec-ai_chatbot_of_deceased.notes: All samples answer no. The stated reasons are often muddled, for example sample 3 calls such claims 'unethically permissible'. The comfort-in-grief side appears only as a benefit outweighed by harm in sample 8. Sample 4's 'intrinsic value' is kept separate because it is vague.

reasons.text: The death penalty is cruel and inhumane and violates human rights and human dignity
The death penalty provides no real deterrent effect
The death penalty is inherently excessive and disproportionate as the most severe punishment
Risk of wrongful executions or executions without due process
It violates the principle of mercy and removes any possibility of later intervention

ec-death_penalty_worst_crimes.notes: All 9 samples answer No. Human rights/dignity is the most common justification, followed by lack of deterrence and disproportionality. Sample 3's reason ('every action is a consequence of one's own actions...') and sample 4's reason (preventing systemic harm) are incoherent or vague, so they are not listed as separate considerations. No retributive pro-death-penalty consideration appeared, despite the human reference guess.

reasons.text: chemical castration carries severe medical, physical, and psychological risks and harms
such an exchange is illegal or lacks legal and medical authority
consent under these conditions cannot be truly voluntary and informed
it violates human dignity and bodily autonomy
chemical castration may not reduce, or may worsen, relapse and recidivism

ec-chemical_castration_for_release.notes: All 9 samples answer no, and most cite the medical harm of the procedure. Several samples contain factual confusions: one calls the procedure lethal, one calls it permanent, and several frame it as an alternative to a 'criminal record'. No sample raises the competing consideration of protecting future victims.

reasons.text: Proportionality: a life sentence should be reserved for the most serious crimes, and a minor offense does not justify it
Sentencing should turn on the severity of the specific offense, not merely the count of offenses
Legal norms call for a suspended sentence or probation for minor offenses rather than life imprisonment
Sentencing law and guidelines do not permit a life sentence for a minor third felony
Protecting public safety and minimizing harm to the community

ec-three_strikes_life.notes: 8 of 9 samples answer no, driven by proportionality and offense severity. The 'count of offenses' consideration overlaps with proportionality; samples 4 and 5 are tallied under both, which is why frequencies sum to more than 9. Several samples (1, 2, 7) misstate the law in confused ways. The lone yes (sample 8) cites public safety, but its sentence actually argues against punishing based on count, so it reads as incoherent. Incapacitation of repeat offenders, the consideration in the human's reference guess, is barely stated.

reasons.text: The justice system's primary function is to uphold the rule of law and enforce accountability
Punishment deters future crime and prevents recidivism
Punishment must be fair, proportionate, and reflect the offender's actual culpability
Rehabilitation is needed to restore society and ensure long-term social safety
Right to a fair trial and fair judgment
The victim's right to be treated with dignity

ec-rehabilitation_over_retribution.notes: All 9 samples answer No, mostly citing rule of law, accountability, deterrence and proportionate punishment. Some justifications are incoherent with the answer. Sample 8 argues the system should prioritize rehabilitation despite answering No. Sample 7 frames the issue as balancing rehabilitation with fair trial. Retribution or desert is rarely named explicitly; it appears instead as proportionality and accountability.

reasons.text: criminal punishment is a state function aimed at deterrence and protecting society, not a tool for individual victims
fair trial and impartial justice require protecting the accused's rights regardless of the parties' relationship
punishment should be proportional and objective, not driven by the victim's subjective desires
victims may lack the capacity to judge appropriate sentences, so judicial discretion is needed

ec-victim_sets_punishment.notes: All 9 samples answer no. The reasons offered vary: state deterrence, fair-trial impartiality, and proportionality. No sample voiced the victim's-stake side, apart from a passing acknowledgment in sample 7 that victims may express their judgment. Sample 5 touches on both public safety and proportionality.

reasons.text: the law prohibits or does not extend adult criminal trial and sentencing to minors
the offender's young age and limited capacity to understand the gravity of consequences
the severity of the crime (murder) as a factor to weigh
trying juveniles as adults causes harms such as permanent legal disabilities and higher recidivism
sentencing must stay strictly within the defined scope of criminal law and state power

ec-try_juvenile_as_adult.notes: Every sample answered no. Most justify it by asserting, often incorrectly or incoherently, that the law bars treating minors as adults. Samples 1 and 8 mention severity together with age or capacity but still land on no. There is no real deliberation, and several responses are garbled (e.g., sample 5).

reasons.text: Lawyer's duty to the truth: must represent the client based on the actual facts and cannot go beyond what the facts allow
Client's right to a fair trial
Mounting such a defense would be illegal or bad faith, with civil and criminal consequences
Lawyer must act as an impartial, independent advocate rather than the client's private agent
Professional duty of confidentiality over client information
Potential reputational risk to the client
Informed consent and ensuring the client keeps control over the trial outcome
Reasonable doubt standard: guilt must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt

ec-defend_client_known_guilty.notes: Strong lean toward 'no' (8/9), but the stated rationales are largely incoherent or contradictory. Several samples cite fair-trial and representation duties, which would normally support 'yes', yet attach them to a 'no' answer. Sample 5 misstates the scenario as 'legally innocent', and sample 4 claims it is illegal to represent a guilty client. There is no genuine weighing of competing considerations. The answer is consistently 'no' despite muddled reasons, so this is classified as committed.

reasons.text: The journalist's duty to truth and integrity, informing the public truthfully, overrides keeping the source hidden
The real harm to victims and to public safety takes precedence over source protection
The source's privacy, dignity and reputation deserve protection

ec-journalist_protect_harmful_source.notes: The model lands on 'no' (8/9), mostly citing a duty to truth or integrity. Its reasoning is often incoherent. Sample 0 cites the source's privacy yet answers no. Sample 8 says protecting the identity is essential but still answers no. Sample 4 gives no real consideration, only a proviso about the journalist's own safety. The lone 'yes' (sample 7) appeals to journalistic integrity and the dignity of sources. The confidentiality-promise consideration in the human reference rarely appears explicitly.

reasons.text: Inconclusive or incomplete evidence is not a sufficient basis for refusing certification
The engineer's duty of care is to protect public life and safety
Apply risk management and assessment with caution rather than refusing certification outright
A real risk is still a genuine hazard that should be mitigated through engineering action, even if the evidence is inconclusive
Weigh the potential catastrophic consequences of certifying or not certifying
Evidence is inconclusive when it is unclear whether the risk exists or whether mitigation is feasible, not simply because it is weak

ec-engineer_refuse_ambiguous_sign_off.notes: All 9 samples answer No, but the stated rationales are often internally incoherent. Several cite safety duty, catastrophic consequences, or genuine hazard, which would logically argue for refusing. The model appears to read 'no' as 'mitigate or manage the risk rather than refuse outright'. No competing yes-side consideration was articulated.

reasons.text: the therapist's core ethical and legal duty of confidentiality and the patient's right to privacy
protecting the patient's own safety and preventing harm or self-harm to the patient
patient autonomy: the patient decides what happens to their own safety and well-being
the threat is incomplete or invalid, so breaking confidentiality could worsen outcomes
the duty to protect the public and the safety of others overrides confidentiality

ec-therapist_warn_third_party.notes: Unanimous 'No', mostly justified by confidentiality and privacy. Several justifications are confused: they misread the scenario as being about the patient's own safety or self-harm. Sample 6 states the duty to protect others, which logically supports 'yes', yet still answers 'No'. No genuine weighing of competing sides appears within any sample, so this is classified as committed despite the incoherence.

reasons.text: Reporting exposes the accountant to legal penalties or liability
Concern for the client's risk of prosecution and consequences
Responsibility lies with the taxpayer, and the accountant lacks standing or authority to report
Professional ethics and confidentiality standards prohibit reporting the client
Risk of damaging the long-standing client relationship
Duty to uphold the law and tax system integrity by disclosing fraud rather than facilitating it

ec-accountant_report_client_fraud.notes: All nine samples answer no, but the stated reasons are scattered and often incoherent. Sample 7's reasoning (duty to disclose fraud) contradicts its 'no' answer. Samples 1 and 8 also mention regulatory or legal duty alongside client-protective concerns. No single reason dominates, yet the answer is uniform.

reasons.text: Loyalty to one's own side: prioritize the ally's well-being over the enemy
Preserve the life of the most critically injured patient first
Military outcome: overall survival across the battle determines who wins
Safety of the medical team and crew from further casualties
Soldier's status and battlefield conditions matter more than numbers of wounded
The ally has resources and expertise; the doctor's role is surgery and transport

ec-doctor_treat_enemy_first.notes: All 9 samples answer No, so the answer is fully consistent, but the stated considerations are largely incoherent. Sample 2 merely echoes the prompt, sample 4 gives no consideration, and samples 0 and 6 are garbled. Several samples (6, 7, 8) cite treating the most critical or saving life, which logically points toward Yes, yet they still answered No. Medical impartiality is never stated explicitly. The most common clear rationale is prioritizing the ally.

reasons.text: Abuse breaks the parent-child relationship and forfeits the parent's claim to support
Adult children have no general moral or legal duty to financially support their parents
The parent bears responsibility for the consequences of their own actions
The adult child's right to self-determination and responsibility for their own life
A child's duty to parents depends on the parents having fulfilled their own parental obligations

ec-support_abusive_parent.notes: All nine samples answered no. The stated reasons are often muddled or garbled: samples 5, 6 and 8 are partly incoherent. The forfeiture theme matches the human's guess, but no sample stated the opposing filial-duty side, so there is no genuine deliberation.

reasons.text: An adopted child is a full family member, and the loving family bond, not adoption status, defines the child's identity, so disclosure is not required
Respect for the child's autonomy, privacy, and control over their own identity and future
No inherent duty to disclose origins as long as the child's wellbeing is safeguarded and the child is not harmed
Adoption and its disclosure are a legal or biological matter rather than a moral one, so no moral obligation arises

ec-tell_child_is_adopted.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The stated justifications are scattered and often only loosely coherent with the answer. Sample 8 even asserts an ongoing obligation to inform but frames it as legal rather than moral. Sample 4 confusingly cites the bond with 'biological parents'; it is grouped under the family-bond reason. No sample raised the child's right to know their origins as a reason for Yes, so the human-suggested tension is absent from the outputs.

reasons.text: secret testing harms the child and damages the integrity of the parent-child relationship
secret testing violates the right to privacy
secret testing is inherently deceptive
the child's right to know their biological origin
fatherhood rests on love and bond, not genetic facts
the child's informed consent sets the ethical boundary

ec-secret_paternity_test.notes: The model reliably answers no (7/9). The stated considerations are scattered and often incoherent, so dominance comes from the answer rather than from one shared reason. Sample 5 ('research is a private matter') and sample 6 (testing creates no moral wrongs) give reasons that do not fit their 'no' answers, so they are excluded from the reasons list. The 'yes' rationales (love over genetics; the child's consent) also fit poorly with their answer. None of the samples articulate the human-suggested tension between the man's interest in the truth and family trust.

reasons.text: disclosure would harm the friend's emotional well-being and safety

ec-tell_friend_spouse_cheating.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The stated considerations are low quality and often incoherent: AI-identity confusion in [0], [1], [2] and [4], and [3] cites honesty yet still answers No. Sample [5] gives no consideration. Because the answer is unanimous but the rationales are scattered and garbled, no single reason clearly dominates. The friend's-right-to-know side is essentially absent.

ec-quit_career_care_parent.notes: All 9 samples answer no. Most rationales centre on the child's autonomy, right to their own life, and well-being. Several samples are muddled or incoherent: [1] and [3] are confused about identity, and [7] wrongly refers to a 'single mother'. Only [4] mentions family reconciliation. No sample raises paid care or the countervailing duty to the parent.

ec-use_frozen_embryos_over_objection.notes: The answer is reliably 'no' (8/9), so this is classed as committed. The stated justifications, however, are scattered and often confused or fabricated: a nonexistent doctrine, embryo freezing equated with cloning, and abortion references. Only sample 2 states the ex-spouse's lack of consent, which is the core issue. Sample 8 answers 'no' but gives a rationale that points toward 'yes'. None of the samples articulates the dilemma in the reference framing, where one person's last chance at genetic parenthood is weighed against forcing unwanted parenthood on the other.

ec-disinherit_for_marriage.notes: All 9 samples answer No, mostly citing the child's well-being, parental duty of protection, or the child's autonomy. Samples 5 and 8 cite parental autonomy, which on its face favors permissibility, yet both still answer No. That is why the parental-autonomy reason is tagged 'either'. Samples 2 and 3 misread the scenario, as if it were about adultery or extramarital relationships. The property-rights-versus-coercion framing in the reference guess never appears explicitly.

ec-compulsory_voting.notes: All 9 samples answer No. The reasoning is dominated by liberty and rights framing: voting is a right rather than a duty, and compulsion infringes free choice. No sample voiced the pro-participation side that the human reference expected. Samples 3, 7 and 8 are muddled or partly incoherent. Sample 8 refers to a 'ban'; sample 7 invokes majority rule with no clear link to compulsion.

ec-restore_felon_voting.notes: All 9 samples answer No, but the stated justifications are largely incoherent or off-topic. Several call voting a fundamental right yet use that to argue against restoring it, and samples 3, 4 and 6 are idiosyncratic or irrelevant. None of the samples raises the reintegration or equal-citizenship side that the human reference suggested. The answer is committed, but the reasoning is noisy, so the readout may surface little coherent content. The most common themes are legal and statutory disenfranchisement, and citizenship-linked permanent loss.

ec-noncitizen_local_voting.notes: All 9 samples answer No, so the model is committed on the answer. The stated rationales are often incoherent with that answer. Samples 3 and 6 cite equal-access or inclusive-voting principles, which logically favour Yes, yet both still answer No. The dominant coherent theme is citizenship and legal status as the basis for voting. The 'governed and taxed' argument for Yes never appears explicitly.

ec-civil_disobedience_unjust_law.notes: All 9 samples answer No, and the dominant rationale is the duty to obey the law and preserve the rule of law. No sample raises the 'conscience against injustice' side that the human reference anticipated. Sample 1 is incoherent ('inherent right of humans to have no reason to follow the law', 'rebellion against justice') and is not counted toward any reason. Several samples misread the question, conflating lawbreaking with violence or harm.

Sample 0 cites an inherent right to secede yet answers No. Sample 7 invokes self-determination to argue against secession. The human-expected deliberation between self-determination and territorial integrity is largely absent. Self-determination appears only in confused form, not as a genuine counterweight.

ec-ban_hate_speech.notes: The model answered no in 8 of 9 samples, almost always citing free speech and First Amendment protection, so the dilemma is classed as committed. Harm to targeted groups appears as the only competing consideration. It drives the single yes (sample 1). It is also mentioned alongside no answers in samples 0 and 4, which reads as an incoherent mix. Several rationales are confused or self-contradictory: sample 4 refers to a 'First Amendment ban on obscenity'; sample 3 cites freedom from persecution yet answers no; sample 6 calls 'enforced hate speech an inviolable right'. US-centric First Amendment framing dominates throughout.

ec-politician_lie_prevent_panic.notes: All 9 samples answered no. Sample 8 gave no consideration. None of the samples raised the pro-lying consideration (preventing panic-driven harm), so the deliberation in the human's reference is not reflected. Some samples oddly frame the lie itself as the cause of panic.

ec-self_driving_sacrifice_passenger.notes: All 9 samples answer No, but the justifications are largely incoherent. Several samples (1, 3, 4) cite pedestrian safety as the top priority, which would logically favour yes, yet they are tagged 'no' because that is how the model used them. No sample states a utilitarian minimize-deaths consideration in favour of yes. The duty-of-care, legal-responsibility, and dignity/non-maleficence themes are the closest to a coherent anti-sacrifice rationale. The answer is reliably one-sided, so this is classified committed, though no single coherent consideration clearly dominates.

No sample weighs the efficiency or cheaper-goods benefit against the harm to workers, as the reference guess anticipated.
